editorial.headline: Wholesale Sea Transport Equipment: Nationally Open, Bali PMA Blocked
editorial.standfirst: This wholesale activity is nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, but Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium blocks registration there.
editorial.body:
This activity covers wholesale trade in a range of sea transport equipment, whether motorised or non-motorised. Its scope also expressly includes the wholesale trade of spare parts and equipment for that transport. The definition therefore holds the principal equipment and its supporting commercial inventory together: sea-transport equipment on one side, and the parts and accessories used with it on the other. It is a wholesale activity with a deliberately broad product frame, rather than a narrow description of one vessel type or one particular component.

The record makes the activity available at every listed business scale: Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar. That is an important part of the classification’s practical shape. A business operating at any of those stated scales can fall within the activity’s scope when its work is the wholesale trade described here. The scale listing is broad, while the commercial subject remains specific: the wholesale supply of varied marine transport equipment, including both motorised and non-motorised forms, plus related spare parts and equipment.

For foreign investment at the national level, the position is open. The PMA status is TERBUKA, and the national foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%. In plain English, the record permits full foreign ownership nationally for this activity. That national position should be read as a national ownership setting, supported by the cited Perpres sources, rather than as an assurance that every Indonesian location applies the same PMA registration outcome.

Bali is the decisive local exception. Today, this activity cannot be registered as PMA in Bali by a foreign investor. The record states that, at the Besar scale, OSS risk is Rendah or Menengah-Rendah across every scope; Bali’s moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis. National openness is not a substitute for Bali eligibility: in Bali, the moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity. The distinction is sharp but straightforward—100% foreign ownership is the national ceiling, while Bali’s current risk-based moratorium prevents PMA registration there.
